prompt.content: A man in his 30s with unresectable rectal adenocarcinoma was undergoing a first cycle of combination chemotherapy that included a continuous infusion of a fluoropyrimidine agent together with a platinum agent and folinic acid. He had been classified as low cardiovascular risk at baseline, with a normal electrocardiogram and unremarkable laboratory tests prior to starting treatment. During the final hours of the continuous infusion he developed abdominal pain, nausea, and palpitations. Electrocardiography showed atrial fibrillation with a rapid ventricular response (rate 150 bpm) and diffuse ST-segment elevation, more pronounced in the lateral leads, prompting immediate discontinuation of the infusion. Ten minutes later he spontaneously converted to sinus rhythm at 93 bpm, with persistent ST-segment elevation and no reciprocal changes. He remained haemodynamically stable throughout, with normal blood pressure, adequate peripheral perfusion, and no elevated lactate on arterial blood gas. Transthoracic echocardiography revealed severe biventricular systolic dysfunction (left ventricular ejection fraction 27%, fractional area change 27%, TAPSE 11 mm, global longitudinal strain −10%), global hypokinesia, and severe mitral regurgitation. Laboratory testing showed markedly elevated troponin (852 ng/L; reference <47), NT-proBNP (3115 ng/L; reference <150), and mildly elevated CRP (0.66 mg/dL), out of proportion to the brief, spontaneously resolved arrhythmia. Urgent coronary angiography demonstrated normal coronary arteries without obstructive disease. Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging subsequently showed a reduced ejection fraction (35%), diffusely elevated native T1 and T2 mapping values, and a subepicardial pattern of late gadolinium enhancement in the basal inferior and inferolateral segments. Immunological, thrombophilic, and virological work-up was unremarkable.

prompt.content: A woman in her early 50s with baseline visual impairment was brought to the emergency department by wheelchair with severe lower back pain (10/10) and mild chest discomfort that had resolved with analgesia prior to arrival. Her family reported a recent inpatient admission for a suspected demyelinating disorder, during which she underwent lumbar puncture and received high-dose corticosteroids; that admission was complicated by a drop in platelet count attributed to heparin exposure, for which heparin products were avoided. Past medical history included hypertension and type 2 diabetes mellitus. She denied limb swelling, fever, hemoptysis, or new neurological symptoms. On arrival, heart rate was 110 beats/min, blood pressure 100/75 mmHg, oxygen saturation 94% on room air, and respiratory rate was initially charted as normal but on manual recount was 31 breaths/min. ECG showed sinus tachycardia. Chest auscultation revealed mild bibasal crackles. Point-of-care lung ultrasound showed a symmetric lung-sliding pattern with vertical lines in all zones bilaterally. Venous compression ultrasound of the lower limb showed a non-compressible right common femoral vein containing intraluminal echogenic material. Given the recent platelet-drop history, an oral anticoagulant was started, and CT pulmonary angiography was obtained, showing filling defects within the right main and left lower lobe pulmonary arterial branches. Initial bloodwork showed leukocytosis (16.53×10^9/L) with neutrophilia and lymphopenia, platelets 123×10^9/L, markedly elevated D-dimer (5.98 mg/L), elevated troponin T (31.18 ng/L), CRP 213.34 mg/L, glucose 9.90 mmol/L, and lactate 3.50 mmol/L.

prompt.content: A man in his early 30s with no known prior thyroid disease presented to the emergency department with acute-onset palpitations, chest discomfort, shortness of breath, recurrent vomiting, and agitation developing over a short period. Past history included mild intermittent bronchial asthma managed with an inhaled budesonide-formoterol combination. There was no history of chronic liver disease, acetaminophen exposure, or prior episodes of hypotension or shock. He was a non-smoker, did not drink alcohol, had no known drug allergies, and had no family history of thyroid or autoimmune disease. On examination he was febrile, markedly tachycardic, and clinically dehydrated, restless and agitated but without focal neurological deficits; there were no peripheral signs of heart failure, no palpable goiter, and no thyroid tenderness. The initial ECG showed a regular narrow-complex tachycardia consistent with 2:1 atrioventricular conduction, which progressed to an irregular narrow-complex tachyarrhythmia; synchronized cardioversion restored sinus rhythm after energy escalation. Bedside echocardiography showed a hyperdynamic circulation without wall motion abnormality or valvular disease, with findings suggesting intravascular volume depletion. Arterial blood gas showed near-normal pH with mild metabolic acidosis and normal lactate. Initial labs showed profound hypokalemia, hypernatremia, and hypercalcemia, alongside marked transaminitis, evolving coagulopathy, thrombocytopenia, and elevated procalcitonin and CRP prompting empirical antibiotics. Blood and urine cultures were negative. CT head and abdominal ultrasound were unremarkable.

prompt.content: A woman in her thirties presented with a one-month history of distal extremity numbness, fatigue, and hair loss. Initial evaluation revealed hypothyroidism, and she was started on thyroid hormone replacement, with notable improvement in fatigue after over a month of treatment. She subsequently discontinued the medication and developed persistent mild limb numbness and weakness, more pronounced in the lower limbs, which gradually progressed from the feet to the thighs over the following year. She was ultimately admitted for evaluation of severe motor and sensory disturbances in her limbs impairing daily activities, including difficulty holding utensils and maintaining balance, along with new slurred speech. She had no other hospitalizations or specialized treatments prior to admission. Examination showed dysarthria, asymmetric tongue atrophy with fasciculations (left greater than right), and left sternocleidomastoid atrophy with asymmetric weakness on cervical rotation. Flaccid tetraparesis was present, more pronounced distally than proximally, with mild intrinsic hand muscle atrophy, generalized areflexia, reduced pinprick and vibration sensation at the wrists and ankles, sensory ataxia, and a positive Romberg sign. Routine bloodwork, inflammatory markers, and infectious studies were unremarkable. Thyroid studies showed markedly elevated TSH and thyroid autoantibodies with low-normal free thyroxine, and thyroid ultrasound suggested a diffuse process. Cerebrospinal fluid showed elevated protein with normal cell count. Electrodiagnostic studies showed a severe, diffuse, demyelinating sensorimotor polyradiculoneuropathy with additional fibrillation potentials in tongue muscles. Spine and brain MRI were normal; plexus imaging showed nerve root thickening and edema.

Side note: :294 DONE detection requires isinstance(message, dict), which typed verifiers 0.3.1 messages fail, so episodes always run to max_turns (garbage is_completed=false, 12 turns).
